newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam sounds alarm on growing economic headaches.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam sounds alarm on growing economic headaches.

text.p: Vietnam's Communist Party daily on Monday gave an unusually frank account of economic problems now facing the administration and called for a big drive to boost industrial production in the remaining months of the year.
"In recent months, there have been signs of stagnation in business and production, worrying problems have appeared," the party mouthpiece Nhan Dan said in an editorial.
It said the growth of output in some industries was low and there were serious stockpiles of commodities such as steel, iron, cement and paper.
Unsuitable imports, a failure to tackle smuggling and the local currency's stability against the dollar had taken the country's trade deficit to a "danger level", the paper said.
Furthermore, falling consumer prices were causing difficulties for producers and although banks were flush with cash, businesses were reluctant to borrow because interest rates were high.
The tone of the editorial contrasted with officials' recent comments and the usual tone of the official media, which generally paints a picture of economic success.

The Foreign Ministry's spokesman said last week that Hanoi was not overly worried about the ballooning trade deficit because most of the country's imports are capital goods for future production and potential exports.

Vietnam posted a record trade deficit of $3.25 billion in the first eight months of this year. Imports leapt 45 percent from the same period of 1995 to $7.60 billion while exports rose by half as much to $4.35 billion.

On Friday, the deputy prime minister in charge of economic affairs said Vietnam was in a good position achieve its targets of 9-10 percent gross domestic product (GDP) growth and 14-14.5 percent industrial output growth this year.
However, Deputy Prime Minister Tran Duc Luong indicated concern about a recent drop in consumer prices and said measures may have to be taken to prevent deflation.
Consumer prices have fallen every month since May, leaving the annual rate of inflation at 3.2 percent last month compared with 18.4 percent a year earlier.
A decade of capitalist-style reforms, foreign aid and the opening of doors to foreign investment have brought an economic boom to Vietnam, where GDP growth has topped eight percent a year since 1992.
The government has set a target of 9-10 percent GDP growth annually between now and 2000 and has objected to foreign press reports suggesting that the economy is cooling down.
